text: So I made up my mind not to pay you another painful visit.
For if I cause you pain, who is left to cheer me but the very people I have hurt?
I wrote as I did so that when I came I would not be pained by those who ought to make me rejoice. I was confident about all of you, that my joy is the joy of every one of you.
I wrote to you out of great distress and anguish of heart, with many tears—not to cause you pain, but to let you know how abundantly I love you.
If anyone has caused pain, he has not pained me alone but, in some measure—I do not want to overstate it—all of you.

versions.text: If anyone has caused pain, he has not pained me, but to some degree—not to overstate it—all of you.
versions.explanation: The current wording is hard to follow when read aloud: 'but to some degree ... all of you' leaves the verb unexpressed and the dash-inserted phrase interrupts the flow awkwardly. Paul's point is not that he was untouched but that the offense affected the whole community; 'not me alone but ... all of you' makes the contrast clear while preserving the qualifying aside (ἵνα μὴ ἐπιβαρῶ, 'so as not to be too severe/overstate').

text: The punishment imposed on such a man by the majority is enough.
Now, instead, you should forgive and comfort him, so that he is not overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
So I urge you to reaffirm your love for him.
This is also why I wrote: to test you and see whether you are obedient in everything.
Anyone you forgive, I forgive as well. And what I have forgiven—if there was anything to forgive—I have forgiven for your sake in the presence of Christ,
so that Satan might not outwit us; for we are not ignorant of his schemes.
When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, and a door was opened for me in the Lord,
even so, my spirit could find no rest, because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia.

versions.text: I still had no peace of mind, because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia.
versions.explanation: 'Peace of mind' shifts the Greek τῷ πνεύματί μου ('in my spirit') to a purely mental idiom and loses Paul's characteristic anthropological term. 'My spirit could find no rest' keeps ἄνεσιν ('relief, rest') and πνεῦμα while still reading naturally aloud.

text: But thanks be to God, who always leads us in his triumphal procession in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of him.

versions.text: But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of him.
versions.explanation: θριαμβεύοντι ἡμᾶς draws on the image of a Roman triumphal procession in which God leads his people along; 'leads us in triumph' can be misread as 'makes us victorious.' Making the procession image explicit preserves the metaphor that also grounds the incense/fragrance imagery in the following verses. A footnote could note the alternative sense, 'causes us to triumph.'

text: For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing:
to the one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. And who is equal to such a task?
For we are not like so many, peddling the word of God for profit. On the contrary, we speak in Christ with sincerity, as sent from God and standing in his presence.
